newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Conservatives narrow Labour's lead - poll.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Conservatives narrow Labour's lead - poll.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservatives narrowed Labour's lead according to the latest opinion polls, but the opposition party was still 14 points ahead, the Guardian newspaper said on Wednesday.
The ICM survey put Labour at 46 points, down two from last month, the Conservatives at 32 (up two) and the Liberal Democrats at 17 (up one), one month before the May 1 election.
"The swing to the Conservatives was mirrored in the monthly unadjusted opinion poll findings, which take no account of voters' relative reluctance to admit to voting Tory," the Guardian said.

The poll, taken over the Easter weekend, showed that the latest series of sleaze allegations against the Conservatives had not damaged the party as much as many people had expected, and that strong economic figures were giving the party a boost.
But it also revealed that public opinion wants the Conservatives implicated in the "cash for questions" scandal to quit as election candidates.

Ten Conservative MPs are under investigation by a parliamentary committee over allegations that they accepted hefty undeclared cash sums in exchange for asking questions in the House of Commons (lower house).
Neil Hamilton, who is accused of accepting money from the owner of Harrods luxury department store, Mohammed Al-Fayed, resisted calls by senior officials to resign.
Another Conservative MP implicated in the "cash for questions" row resigned last week while two stood down in reaction to accusations of involvement in sexual scandals.
Eighty-one percent of the 1,200 people questioned for the poll said the MPs in the sleaze row should quit and only 14 percent said they should stand for election again.

A poll in the daily paper The Scotsman showed the Conservatives gaining three points, supporting the ICM survey findings. It put the Conservatives at 20 points while Labour remained steady at 47 and the Scottish National Party at 23.
"Labour's position remains far stronger than at the equivalent stage in the 1992 campaign," the Guardian said.
